The foundational premise posits that behavior-situations possess an intrinsic 'field-character', implying that learning does not occur in isolation but rather through interactions among sign-gestalts within a broader environmental context. This leads to the concept of mutual reinforcement, where the acquisition of one alternative influences others due to their interdependence within the same field. The resulting expectation field dynamics suggest that learning outcomes depend not only on individual stimuli but also on how these stimuli relate to each other in time and space. These principles form a dualistic structure: on one hand, the individual sign-gestalt learns independently, while on the other, its trajectory is shaped by the collective field. This duality manifests in failure modes such as interference effects or premature convergence when field dependencies are overlooked. The mathematical implication is that traditional models treating alternatives as independent entities fail to capture the full complexity of learning processes, necessitating a shift toward field-based probabilistic frameworks.
